verses.zh: 过了些日子，到割麦子的时候，参孙带着一只山羊羔去看他的妻，说：「我要进内室见我的妻。」他岳父不容他进去，
verses.en: Sometime later, during the wheat harvest,[NOTE:1] Samson took a young goat as a gift and went to visit his bride.[NOTE:2] He said to her father,[NOTE:3] “I want to sleep with[NOTE:4] my bride in her bedroom!”[NOTE:5] But her father would not let him enter.
notes: The wheat harvest took place during the month of May. See O. Borowski, Agriculture in Iron Age Israel, 37, 88.
Heb “Samson visited his wife with a young goat.”
The words “to her father” are supplied in the translation (see the end of the verse).
Heb “I want to approach.” The verb בּוֹא (boʾ) with the preposition אֶל (ʾel) means “come to” or “approach,” but is also used as a euphemism for sexual relations.

Heb “I will go to my wife in the bedroom.” The Hebrew idiom בּוֹא אֶל (boʾ ʾel, “to go to”) often has sexual connotations. The cohortative form used by Samson can be translated as indicating resolve (“I want to go”) or request (“let me go”).
verses.commentary:
15:1 "in the time of wheat harvest" This would be May or June.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANCIENT NEAR EASTERN CALENDARS

▣ "visited his wife" Samson believed he was still married. Apparently the marriage arrangement was for
his Philistine wife to reside with her parents and he would visit from time to time.

▣ "with a young goat" This would be for a celebratory dinner.

verses.zh: 说：「我估定你是极其恨她，因此我将她给了你的陪伴。她的妹子不是比她还美丽吗？你可以娶来代替她吧！」
verses.en: Her father said, “I really thought[NOTE:1] you absolutely despised[NOTE:2] her, so I gave her to your best man. Her younger sister is more attractive than she is. Take her instead!”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “saying, I said.” The first person form of אָמַר (ʾamar, “to say”) sometimes indicates self-reflection. The girl’s father uses the infinitive absolute for emphasis.
Heb “hating, you hated.” Once again the girl’s father uses the infinitive absolute for emphasis.
Heb “Is her younger sister not better than her? Let her [i.e., the younger sister] be yours instead of her [i.e., Samson’s ‘bride’]).”
verses.commentary:
15:2 This verse has two intensified grammatical forms (i.e., two INFINITIVE ABSOLUTES
with a PERFECT VERB from the same root).

- "I really thought" (lit. "say") ‒ BDB 55, KB 65

- "hated her intensely" ‒ BDB 971, KB 1338

▣ "I gave her to your companion" This would have been one of the thirty Philistine wedding friends (cf.
Jdgs. 14:10-11). See notes at Jdgs. 14:20.

▣ "Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she" Either the father was trying to correct an
unfortunate mistake or he was trying to keep the dowry. Notice the motive is still on outward beauty (i.e., Jdgs. 14:3, 7).

verses.zh: 参孙说：「这回我加害于非利士人不算有罪。」
verses.en: Samson said to them,[NOTE:1] “This time I am justified in doing the Philistines harm!”[NOTE:2]
notes: Codex Alexandrinus (A) of the (original) LXX has the singular “to him.”
Heb “I am innocent this time from the Philistines when I do with them harm.”
verses.commentary:
15:3 Obviously there had been some blowback from his slaughter of thirty men from Ashkelon (i.e., Jdgs.
14:19). Apparently this push-back came from both the Judeans and the Philistines.

The VERB (BDB 667, KB 720, Niphal PERFECT) can refer to

- free from punishment (often expressed in the negative) ‒ Exod. 21:19; Num. 5:28; 1 Sam. 26:9; Pro. 6:29; 11:21; 16:5;
17:5; 19:5, 9; 28:20; Jer. 25:29; 49:12

- free from quiet ‒ Num. 5:31; Ps. 19:14; Jer. 2:39

verses.zh: 于是参孙去捉了三百只狐狸（或译：野狗），将狐狸尾巴一对一对地捆上，将火把捆在两条尾巴中间，
verses.en: Samson went and captured 300 jackals[NOTE:1] and got some torches. He tied the jackals in pairs by their tails and then tied a torch to each pair.[NOTE:2]
notes: Traditionally, “foxes.”
Heb “He turned tail to tail and placed one torch between the two tails in the middle.”
verses.commentary:
15:4 "foxes" This same Hebrew word (BDB 1043) can refer to "jackals." Foxes were an idiom for "problems"
(i.e., "harvest problems," cf. Song of Songs 2:15).

verses.zh: 点着火把，就放狐狸进入非利士人站着的禾稼，将堆集的禾捆和未割的禾稼，并橄榄园尽都烧了。
verses.en: He lit the torches[NOTE:1] and set the jackals loose in the Philistines’ standing grain. He burned up the grain heaps and the standing grain, as well as the vineyards and olive groves.
notes: Heb “He set fire to the torches.”
verses.commentary:
15:5 "the shocks and the standing grain, along with the vineyards and groves" The "shocks" (BDB 155 I) refers
to the stacks of cut grain or sheaves (unwrapped, i.e., it was the wheat harvest, Jdgs. 15:1), while "standing grain" (BDB 879)
refers to

- uncut grain

- not yet ripe grain

This was a disaster for an agricultural community, not only because of the loss of that year's food and seed
crop, but also this meant permanently, because fire damage to the vines and trees had taken so long to bring into cultivation.

verses.zh: 非利士人说：「这事是谁做的呢？」有人说：「是亭拿人的女婿参孙，因为他岳父将他的妻给了他的陪伴。」于是非利士人上去，用火烧了妇人和她的父亲。
verses.en: The Philistines asked,[NOTE:1] “Who did this?” They were told,[NOTE:2] “Samson, the Timnite’s son-in-law, because the Timnite[NOTE:3] took Samson’s[NOTE:4] bride and gave her to his best man.” So the Philistines went up and burned her and her father.[NOTE:5]
notes: Or “said.”
Heb “and they said.” The subject of the plural verb is indefinite.
Heb “he”; the referent (the Timnite) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “his”; the referent (Samson) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

The Hebrew text expands the statement with the additional phrase “burned with fire.” The words “with fire” are redundant in English and have been omitted from the translation for stylistic reasons. Some textual witnesses read “burned…her father’s house,” perhaps under the influence of 14:15. On the other hand, the shorter text may have lost this phrase due to haplography.
verses.commentary:
15:6 "burned her and her father with fire" What irony (cf. Jdgs. 14:15)! The Philistines did this to appease Samson
but it made him madder (cf. Jdgs. 15:7)! The LXX adds "burned her father's house," which the Peshitta understands as
"burned her father's family."

verses.zh: 参孙对非利士人说：「你们既然这样行，我必向你们报仇才肯罢休。」
verses.en: Samson said to them, “Because you did this,[NOTE:1] I will get revenge against you before I quit fighting.”[NOTE:2]
notes: The Niphal of נָקָם (naqam, “to avenge, to take vengeance”) followed by the preposition ב (bet) has the force “to get revenge against.” See 1 Sam 18:25; Jer 50:15; Ezek 25:12.
Heb “and afterward I will stop.”

verses.zh: 参孙就大大击杀他们，连腿带腰都砍断了。他便下去，住在以坦磐的穴内。
verses.en: He struck them down and defeated them.[NOTE:1] Then he went down and lived for a time in the cave in the cliff of Etam.
notes: Heb “He struck them, calf on thigh, [with] a great slaughter.” The precise meaning of the phrase “calf on thigh” is uncertain.
verses.commentary:
15:8 "struck them relentlessly" This is literally "hip and thigh." It must have been a Semitic proverb. The thigh
muscle is the strongest in the human body and is often used as a symbol of strength.

▣ "lived in the cleft of the rock of Etam" The MacMillan Bible Atlas places this site south of Bethlehem
on the main road, close to the foothills of Judah (maps #119, 140).

It was a well protected cleft on a well known rock. The Philistines could not easily surprise him there.

verses.zh: 非利士人上去安营在犹大，布散在利希。
verses.en: The Philistines went up and invaded[NOTE:1] Judah. They arrayed themselves for battle[NOTE:2] in Lehi.
notes: Or “camped in.”
Or “spread out.” The Niphal of נָטָשׁ (natash) has this same sense in 2 Sam 5:18, 22.
verses.commentary:
15:9 "the Philistines went up and camped in Judah" This shows this had become an international incident (i.e.,
Jdgs. 15:5). Samson's actions were serious and a retaliatory strike was undertaken by the Philistines.

▣ "Lehi" This verse clearly shows the fear of the Judeans. The name means "jawbone" (BDB 534 II, cf.
Jdgs. 15:15).

The location of this place name is uncertain. Scholars suggest it was on the Philistine ‒ Judah border
in the lowlands (cf. ABA, pp. 274-275. It is not even listed in the index of the MacMillan Bible Atlas.

It apparently gets its name from the revenge attack by Samson with the jawbone of a donkey.

verses.zh: 犹大人说：「你们为何上来攻击我们呢？」他们说：「我们上来是要捆绑参孙；他向我们怎样行，我们也要向他怎样行。」
verses.en: The men of Judah said, “Why are you attacking[NOTE:1] us?” The Philistines[NOTE:2] said, “We have come up to take Samson prisoner so we can do to him what he has done to us.”
notes: Or “come up against.”
Heb “they”; the referent (the Philistines) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 于是有三千犹大人下到以坦磐的穴内，对参孙说：「非利士人辖制我们，你不知道吗？你向我们行的是甚么事呢？」他回答说：「他们向我怎样行，我也要向他们怎样行。」
verses.en: So 3,000 men of Judah went down to the cave in the cliff of Etam and said to Samson, “Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? Why have you done this to us?” He said to them, “I have only done to them what they have done to me.”
verses.commentary: 15:11 This was "the" problem that God, through Samson, wanted to highlight (cf. Jdgs. 14:4).

verses.zh: 犹大人对他说：「我们下来是要捆绑你，将你交在非利士人手中。」参孙说：「你们要向我起誓，应承你们自己不害死我。」
verses.en: They said to him, “We have come down to take you prisoner so we can hand you over to the Philistines.” Samson said to them, “Promise me[NOTE:1] you will not kill[NOTE:2] me.”
notes: Or “swear to me.”
Heb “meet [with hostility]”; “harm.” In light of v. 13, “kill” is an appropriate translation.
verses.commentary:
15:12 "Swear to me that you will not kill me" Samson was not afraid but he did not want to hurt his own countrymen
in self-defense. He was afraid of his own power (i.e., the coming of the Spirit).

verses.zh: 他们说：「我们断不杀你，只要将你捆绑交在非利士人手中。」于是用两条新绳捆绑参孙，将他从以坦磐带上去。
verses.en: They said to him, “We promise![NOTE:1] We will only take you prisoner and hand you over to them. We promise not to kill you.” They tied him up with two brand new ropes and led him up from the cliff.
notes: Heb “No,” meaning that they will not harm him.
verses.commentary:
15:13 This verse, like Jdgs. 15:2, has two intensified grammatical forms (i.e., INFINITIVE
ABSOLUTE and IMPERFECT VERB of the same root).

- "bind you fast" ‒ BDB 63, KB 75

- "for surely we will not kill you" ‒ BDB 559, KB 562

These Judeans made a strong promise. You can sense their fear, not only of the Philistines (Jdgs. 15:11)
but also of Samson (i.e., "bound him with two new ropes).

verses.zh: 参孙到了利希，非利士人都迎着喧嚷。耶和华的灵大大感动参孙，他臂上的绳就像火烧的麻一样，他的绑绳都从他手上脱落下来。
verses.en: When he arrived in Lehi, the Philistines shouted as they approached him. But the Lord’s Spirit empowered[NOTE:1] him. The ropes around his arms were like flax dissolving in[NOTE:2] fire, and they[NOTE:3] melted away from his hands.
notes: Heb “rushed on.”
Heb “burned with.”
Heb “his bonds.”
verses.commentary:
15:14 The new ropes of the Judeans are now

- burnt flax

- dropped (NASB), but literally "melted"

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

verses.zh: 他见一块未干的驴腮骨，就伸手拾起来，用以击杀一千人。
verses.en: He happened to see[NOTE:1] a solid[NOTE:2] jawbone of a donkey. He grabbed it[NOTE:3] and struck down[NOTE:4] 1,000 men.
notes: Heb “he found.”
Heb “fresh,” i.e., not decayed and brittle.
Heb “he reached out his hand and took it.”
The Hebrew text adds “with it.” This has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.
verses.commentary:
15:15 "a fresh jawbone" It was not an old, dried out jawbone. The ADJECTIVE "fresh"
(BDB 382) is used only here. These skeletal parts were used as plows and sickles, therefore, there were many of
them. This, like Jdgs. 14:8, would have made him ceremonially unclean. See note at Jdgs. 15:9.

▣ "killed a thousand" This was a round number.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THOUSAND (eleph)

verses.zh: 参孙说：我用驴腮骨杀人成堆，用驴腮骨杀了一千人。
verses.en: Samson then said,“With the jawbone of a donkey I have left them in heaps;[NOTE:1] with the jawbone of a donkey I have struck down a thousand men!”
notes: The precise meaning of the second half of the line (חֲמוֹר חֲמֹרָתָיִם, khamor khamoratayim) is uncertain. The present translation assumes that the phrase means, “a heap, two heaps” and refers to the heaps of corpses littering the battlefield. Other options include: (a) “I have made donkeys of them” (cf. NIV; see C. F. Burney, Judges, 373, for a discussion of this view, which understands a denominative verb from the noun “donkey”); (b) “I have thoroughly skinned them” (see HALOT 330 s.v. IV cj. חמר, which appeals to an Arabic cognate for support); (c) “I have stormed mightily against them,” which assumes the verb חָמַר (khamar, “to ferment; to foam; to boil up”).
verses.commentary:
15:16 This is a word play poem.

- "With the jawbone of an ass, I piled them in mass," Moffatt

- "With the red ass's jawbone, I have reddened them bright red," Barney

verses.zh: 说完这话，就把那腮骨从手里抛出去了。那地便叫拉末・利希。
verses.en: When he finished speaking, he threw the jawbone down[NOTE:1] and named that place Ramath Lehi.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “from his hand.”
The name Ramath Lehi means “Height of the Jawbone.”

verses.zh: 参孙甚觉口渴，就求告耶和华说：「你既藉仆人的手施行这么大的拯救，岂可任我渴死、落在未受割礼的人手中呢？」
verses.en: He was very thirsty, so he cried out to the Lord and said, “You have given your servant[NOTE:1] this great victory. But now must I die of thirst and fall into the hands of these uncircumcised Philistines?”[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “you have placed into the hand of your servant.”
Heb “the hand of uncircumcised.” “Hand” often represents power or control. “The uncircumcised [ones]” is used as a pejorative and in the context refers to the Philistines.
verses.commentary:
15:18-19 This account is much like Elijah's in 1 Kings 19. Samson's faith is seen here more clearly than
other places! Notice, though, Samson gives no glory to God for the victory in Jdgs. 15:16, but here he does. Samson's
perspective is changing but it is still worldly (i.e., Judges 16).

verses.zh: 神就使利希的洼处裂开，有水从其中涌出来。参孙喝了，精神复原；因此那泉名叫隐・哈歌利，那泉直到今日还在利希。
verses.en: So God split open the basin[NOTE:1] at Lehi, and water flowed out from it. When he took a drink, his strength[NOTE:2] was restored and he revived. For this reason he named the spring[NOTE:3] En Hakkore.[NOTE:4] It remains in Lehi to this very day.
notes: The word translated “basin” refers to a circular-shaped depression in the land’s surface.
Heb “spirit.”
Heb “named it”; the referent (the spring) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The name En Hakkore means “Spring of the one who cries out.”
verses.commentary:
15:19 Places often receive their names from events that occurred there.

▣ "strength" This is the Hebrew ruah (BDB 924). There is an obvious word play between

- Samson's spirit

- YHWH's Spirit, Jdgs. 15:14

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

verses.zh: 当非利士人辖制以色列人的时候，参孙作以色列的士师二十年。
verses.en: Samson led[NOTE:1] Israel for 20 years during the days of Philistine prominence.[NOTE:2]
notes: Traditionally, “judged.”
Heb “in the days of the Philistines.”
verses.commentary:
15:20 "he judges Israel twenty years" We have only a small amount of Samson's life recorded. This verse
seems to mark the conclusion of the Samson account, but notice Jdgs. 16:31, where it is repeated. Judges 16 may
be a later edition by the author.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own
interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation.
You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of
the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Why did Samson bring a goat?

- Why did the father think Samson "hated" his daughter?

- Who is "your companion"?

- How does Jdgs. 15:10-11 describe the mental state of the Judeans?

- Why did Samson want the Judeans to swear they would not kill him?

- How does Jdgs. 15:18 reveal Samson's faith?

- Is Jdgs. 15:19 a supernatural event or a local legend? Why?

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: 15:1-8

1But after a while, in the time of wheat harvest, Samson visited his wife with a young goat, and said, "I will go
in to my wife in her room." But her father did not let him enter. 2Her father said, "I really thought that you
hated her intensely; so I gave her to your companion. Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she? Please let her be
yours instead." 3Samson then said to them, "This time I shall be blameless in regard to the Philistines when
I do them harm." 4Samson went and caught three hundred foxes, and took torches, and turned the foxes
tail to tail and put one torch in the middle between two tails. 5When he had set fire to the torches, he released
the foxes into the standing grain of the Philistines, thus burning up both the shocks and the standing grain, along with the
vineyards and groves. 6Then the Philistines said, "Who did this?" And they said, "Samson, the son-in-law of
the Timnite, because he took his wife and gave her to his companion." So the Philistines came up and burned her and her
father with fire. 7Samson said to them, "Since you act like this, I will surely take revenge on you, but after that
I will quit." 8He struck them ruthlessly with a great slaughter; and he went down and lived in the cleft of the rock
of Etam.
